<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par119 />{{GHGpar-heading|119|The Subordination of Nouns to the Verb by means of Prepositions}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|a}}
'''1.''' In general. As is the case with regard to the looser subordination of nouns to the verbal idea (§ 118), so also their subordination by means of prepositions is used to represent the more immediate circumstances (of place, time, cause, purpose, measure, association, or separation) under which an action or event is accomplished. In the case of most prepositions some idea of a relation of ''space'' underlies the construction, which then, in a wider sense, is extended to the ideas of time, motive, or other relations conceived by the mind.

On the origin of the prepositions and the original case-relation in which they stand to the nouns governed by them, cf. § 101, where a list of the prepositions is given with their original meanings. Cf. also § 102 on the prefixes, and § 103 on the union of prepositions with suffixes.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|b}}
'''2.''' A not unimportant part is played in Hebrew by the ''compounding'' of prepositions to represent more accurately the relations of place, which either precede or follow the action. In the former case {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}}, and in the latter (which is not so frequent) {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־}} occurs before other prepositions of place; cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Am|chapter=7|verse=15}} ''the Lord took me'' {{GHGheb|text=מֵאַֽחֲרֵי הַצֹּאן|translate=from behind the flock}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=18}} ''turn thee'' {{GHGheb|text=אֶל־אַֽחֲרָי|translate=to behind me}}, i.e., ''turn thee behind me''; {{GHGheb|text=מֵעִם־}}, {{GHGheb|text=מֵאֵת|translate=from being with}} ..., as in French ''de chez, d’après quelqu’un''.<ref>In other cases French, as well as English and German, can only emphasize ''one'' of the two combined ideas; thus, such expressions as ''il prend le chapeau sur la table'', German and English ''er nimmt den Hut vom Tisch'', ''he takes his hat from the table'', all regard the action from one point of view only; the Hebrew here brings out both aspects of it by means of {{GHGheb|text=מֵעַל־|translate=from upon}}, cf. e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=6|verse=6}}.</ref> For further examples, see ''c''.

{{GHGmargin-letter|119|c}}
Rem. 1. We must ''not'' regard as combined prepositions in the above sense either those ''substantives'' which have become prepositions only by their union with prefixes, as {{GHGheb|text=לִפְנֵי|translate=before}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִפְּנֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=לְמַ֫עַן|translate=on account of}} (but e.g. {{GHGheb|text=מִלִּפְנֵי|translate=from before}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=4|verse=16}}, &c., is such a compound); nor ''adverbs'', which are also formed by combining words which were originally substantives (also used as prepositions) with prepositions, as {{GHGheb|text=מִחוּץ|translate=without}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִתַּ֫חַת}} in the sense of ''below'',<ref>Hence not to be confounded with {{GHGheb|text=מִתַּ֫חַת|translate=from under}}, in such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=22|verse=27}}, which is a real compound preposition. In the above-mentioned adverbs also the {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} was ''originally'' by no means pleonastic; {{GHGheb|text=מִתַּ֫חַת}} denotes properly the locality, regarded primarily as a place ''from beneath'' which something proceeds, and so on. This original sense of the {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}}, however, has become so much obscured by its regular combination with words of place to form independent adverbs, that it is even prefixed (evidently only on the analogy of such common adverbs as {{GHGheb|text=מֵעַל־}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִתַּ֫חַת}}) in cases where it is really inadmissible, owing to the meaning of the adverb, e.g. in {{GHGheb|text=מִבַּלְעֲדֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִלְּבַד|translate=without}}, cf. also such examples as {{GHGheb|text=מִבְּלִי}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִמּוּל}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִנֶּ֫גֶד}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִשָּׁם}} (''there''), &c. Since a {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} is not usually repeated after {{GHGheb|text=מִלְּבַד}}, it appears as if {{GHGheb|text=מִלְּבַד}} by a transposition of the {{GHGheb|text=מִן־}} stood for the usual {{GHGheb|text=לְבַד מִן־}}. In reality, however, the preposition which forms the adverb into a preposition is omitted here, as in {{GHGheb|text=מֵעַל}}, {{GHGheb|text=מִתַּ֫חַת}} without a following {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} (see above). Properly {{GHGheb|text=מִלְּבַד}} has a purely adverbial meaning=''taken by itself'', like {{GHGheb|text=מִלְּמַ֫עְלָה מִמַּ֫עַל}} (Syriac ''men leʿēl'') ''above'' (adv.), as distinguished from {{GHGheb|text=מִמַּ֫עַל לְ}} or {{GHGheb|text=מֵעַל־לְ}} (Syriac ''leʿēl men''), ''over, upon something''.—Also {{GHGheb|text=לְמִן־|translate=from ... onward}} is not for {{GHGheb|text=מִן־לְ}}, but the {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} serves merely (just like the Latin ''usque'' in ''usque a, usque ad, usque ex'') to indicate expressly the starting-point, as an exact ''terminus a quo'' (of place or time).</ref> {{GHGheb|text=מֵעָל}}<section end=par119 /><noinclude>
